paragraphs: We now proceed to examine the judiciary department of the proposed government.

In setting out the defects of the existing Confederation, I made clear the usefulness and necessity of a federal judiciary. I need not review the considerations urged there, because no one disputes that the institution is proper in principle. The only questions raised concern how it is to be constituted and how far its authority is to extend. Our observations will therefore be confined to those two points.

The question of how the judiciary is to be constituted seems to include these separate matters: 1st. The way the judges are appointed. 2d. The terms on which they hold their places. 3d. The division of judicial authority among different courts, and the relations of those courts to each other.

First. As to how the judges are appointed: this is the same as the way the other officers of the Union are appointed, and it was discussed so fully in the last two numbers that anything I said here would be useless repetition.
Second. As to the terms on which the judges hold their places: this chiefly concerns how long they stay in office, the provisions for their support, and the precautions for holding them responsible.

Under the plan of the Convention, all judges appointed by the United States are to hold their offices during good behavior. This is in accordance with the best of the State constitutions, including that of this State. That the adversaries of the plan have questioned the provision is no small sign of the rage for objection that disorders their imaginations and their judgment. The standard of good behavior for keeping judicial office is certainly one of the most valuable of the modern improvements in the practice of government. In a monarchy it is an excellent barrier against the despotism of the prince; in a republic it is an equally excellent barrier against the encroachments and oppressions of the representative body. And it is the best means that can be devised, in any government, of securing a steady, upright and impartial administration of the laws.

Anyone who carefully considers the different departments of power must see that in a government where they are kept separate from one another, the judiciary, by the nature of its functions, will always be the least dangerous to the political rights of the Constitution, because it will be the least able to annoy or injure them. The Executive not only dispenses the honors but holds the sword of the community. The legislature not only controls the purse but prescribes the rules by which the duties and rights of every citizen are to be regulated. The judiciary, by contrast, has no influence over either the sword or the purse; it has no direction of the strength or of the wealth of the society, and can take no active resolution whatever. It may truly be said to have neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment; and in the end it must depend on the executive arm even for the effectiveness of its judgments.

This simple view of the matter suggests several important consequences. It proves beyond question that the judiciary is by far the weakest of the three departments of power(1); that it can never successfully attack either of the other two; and that every possible care is needed to enable it to defend itself against their attacks. It proves equally that although individual oppression may now and then come from the courts of justice, the general liberty of the people can never be endangered from that quarter. I mean this so long as the judiciary remains truly distinct from both the legislature and the Executive. For I agree that "there is no liberty, if the power of judging be not separated from the legislative and executive powers."(2) And it proves, finally, the following. Liberty can have nothing to fear from the judiciary alone, but would have everything to fear from its union with either of the other departments. All the effects of such a union must follow from a dependence of the judiciary on one of the others, despite a nominal and apparent separation. From its natural feebleness the judiciary is in continual danger of being overpowered, awed or influenced by its co-ordinate branches. And nothing can contribute so much to its firmness and independence as permanency in office. This quality may therefore be justly regarded as an indispensable ingredient in its constitution, and in a great measure as the citadel of the public justice and the public security.

Courts of justice must be completely independent above all in a limited Constitution. By a limited Constitution I mean one that sets out certain specific exceptions to the legislative authority; for instance, that the legislature may pass no bills of attainder and no ex post facto laws, and so on. In practice, such limitations can be kept only through courts of justice, whose duty it must be to declare all acts contrary to the manifest tenor of the Constitution void. Without this, every reservation of particular rights or privileges would come to nothing.

Some perplexity about the right of the courts to pronounce legislative acts void because they are contrary to the Constitution has arisen from the notion that this doctrine would imply a superiority of the judiciary to the legislative power. It is argued that the authority that can declare the acts of another void must necessarily be superior to the authority whose acts may be declared void. Since this doctrine is of great importance in all the American constitutions, a brief discussion of the ground it rests on cannot be unwelcome.

No position rests on clearer principles than this: any act of a delegated authority that is contrary to the terms of the commission under which it acts is void. So no legislative act contrary to the Constitution can be valid. To deny this would be to say that the deputy is greater than his principal, that the servant is above his master, that the representatives of the people are superior to the people themselves, and that men acting under granted powers may do not only what those powers do not authorize but even what they forbid.

Suppose it is said that the legislative body is itself the constitutional judge of its own powers, and that its interpretation of them is binding on the other departments. The answer is that this cannot be the natural presumption where no particular provision of the Constitution points to it. Otherwise we cannot suppose that the Constitution meant to enable the representatives of the people to substitute their will for that of their constituents. It is far more reasonable to suppose that the courts were designed to be an intermediate body between the people and the legislature, in order, among other things, to keep the legislature within the limits assigned to its authority. Interpreting the laws is the proper and peculiar province of the courts. A constitution is, in fact, and must be regarded by the judges as, a fundamental law. It therefore belongs to them to determine its meaning, as well as the meaning of any particular act coming from the legislative body. If an irreconcilable conflict should arise between the two, the one with the superior obligation and validity ought of course to be preferred. In other words, the Constitution ought to be preferred to the statute, the intention of the people to the intention of their agents.

Nor does this conclusion in any way suppose that the judicial power is superior to the legislative. It supposes only that the power of the people is superior to both. Where the will of the legislature, declared in its statutes, stands in opposition to that of the people, declared in the Constitution, the judges ought to be governed by the latter rather than the former. They ought to base their decisions on the fundamental laws rather than on those that are not fundamental.

A familiar instance shows this exercise of judicial discretion in choosing between two contradictory laws. It not uncommonly happens that two statutes exist at the same time, clashing in whole or in part, and neither contains any repealing clause or expression. In such a case it is the province of the courts to settle and fix their meaning and operation. As far as they can be reconciled by any fair construction, reason and law together dictate that this should be done. Where that is impracticable, it becomes necessary to give effect to one and exclude the other. The rule the courts have adopted for deciding their relative validity is that the last in order of time shall be preferred to the first. But this is a mere rule of construction. It is derived not from any positive law but from the nature and reason of the thing. It is a rule not imposed on the courts by the legislature, but adopted by the courts themselves as consonant with truth and propriety, to direct their conduct as interpreters of the law. They thought it reasonable that, between the conflicting acts of an EQUAL authority, the one that was the last expression of its will should be preferred.

But where the conflicting acts come from a superior and a subordinate authority, an original and a derivative power, the nature and reason of the thing point to the reverse of that rule. They teach us that the earlier act of a superior ought to be preferred to the later act of an inferior and subordinate authority. Accordingly, whenever a particular statute contravenes the Constitution, it will be the duty of the courts to adhere to the Constitution and disregard the statute.

It carries no weight to say that the courts, on the pretense of a conflict, may substitute their own pleasure for the constitutional intentions of the legislature. This might just as well happen with two contradictory statutes, or in every judgment on any single statute. The courts must declare the sense of the law; and if they were disposed to exercise WILL instead of JUDGMENT, the result would equally be that their pleasure was substituted for that of the legislative body. If this observation proves anything, it proves that there ought to be no judges distinct from that body.

If, then, the courts of justice are to be considered the bulwarks of a limited Constitution against legislative encroachments, this strongly supports permanent tenure for judicial offices. Nothing will contribute so much to that independent spirit in the judges, which is essential to the faithful performance of so arduous a duty.

This independence of the judges is equally necessary to guard the Constitution and the rights of individuals from the effects of those ill humors that the arts of designing men, or the influence of particular conjunctures, sometimes spread among the people themselves. Though these give way quickly to better information and more deliberate reflection, in the meantime they tend to produce dangerous innovations in the government and serious oppressions of the minority in the community. I trust the friends of the proposed Constitution will never join its enemies(3) in questioning that fundamental principle of republican government, which admits the right of the people to alter or abolish the established Constitution whenever they find it inconsistent with their happiness. Yet it does not follow from this principle that the representatives of the people would be justified in violating the provisions of the existing Constitution whenever a momentary inclination, incompatible with those provisions, takes hold of a majority of their constituents. Nor does it follow that the courts would be under a greater obligation to connive at infractions of that kind than at infractions that came wholly from the cabals of the representative body. Until the people have, by some solemn and authoritative act, annulled or changed the established form, it is binding on them collectively as well as individually. No presumption, or even knowledge, of their views can warrant their representatives in departing from it before such an act. But it is easy to see that it would take an uncommon degree of fortitude in the judges to do their duty as faithful guardians of the Constitution where legislative invasions of it had been instigated by the majority voice of the community.

But it is not only with a view to infractions of the Constitution that the independence of the judges may be an essential safeguard against the effects of occasional ill humors in society. These sometimes go no further than injuring the private rights of particular classes of citizens through unjust and biased laws. Here also the firmness of the judges is of vast importance in softening the severity of such laws and confining their operation. It not only serves to moderate the immediate harms of those that may have been passed, but it acts as a check on the legislative body in passing them. Legislators who see that the scruples of the courts will obstruct the success of an unjust intention are in a manner compelled, by the very motives of the injustice they plan, to moderate their attempts. This circumstance is likely to have more influence on the character of our governments than few may realize. The benefits of the integrity and moderation of the judiciary have already been felt in more than one State. Though they may have displeased those whose improper expectations they disappointed, they must have earned the esteem and applause of all the virtuous and disinterested. Thoughtful men of every description ought to value whatever tends to produce or strengthen that disposition in the courts, since no one can be sure that he will not be the victim tomorrow of a spirit of injustice by which he may be a gainer today. And everyone must now feel that the inevitable tendency of such a spirit is to undermine the foundations of public and private confidence, and to put universal distrust and distress in their place.

That inflexible and uniform adherence to the rights of the Constitution and of individuals, which we see to be indispensable in the courts of justice, certainly cannot be expected from judges who hold their offices by a temporary commission. Periodical appointments, however regulated and by whomever made, would in one way or another be fatal to their necessary independence. If the power of making them were committed to the Executive or the legislature, there would be danger of improper compliance toward the branch that held it. If it were committed to both, the judges would be unwilling to risk the displeasure of either. If it were committed to the people, or to persons chosen by them for the purpose, there would be too great a disposition to consult popularity, so that we could not rely on the judges to consult nothing but the Constitution and the laws.

There is a further and weightier reason for permanency in judicial offices, which follows from the nature of the qualifications they require. It has often been remarked, and with great justice, that a voluminous code of laws is one of the drawbacks that necessarily go with the advantages of a free government. To avoid arbitrary discretion in the courts, it is indispensable that they be bound by strict rules and precedents, which define and point out their duty in every particular case that comes before them. It is easy to see, given the variety of controversies that grow out of the folly and wickedness of mankind, that the records of those precedents must inevitably swell to a considerable bulk, and that acquiring a competent knowledge of them demands long and laborious study. Hence few men in the society will have enough skill in the laws to qualify them to be judges. And after making the proper deductions for the ordinary depravity of human nature, the number is smaller still of those who unite the requisite integrity with the requisite knowledge. These considerations show that the government can have no great choice among fit characters. A temporary term in office would naturally discourage such characters from leaving a lucrative practice to take a seat on the bench, and would tend to put the administration of justice into hands less able and less well qualified to conduct it with usefulness and dignity. In the present circumstances of this country, and in those in which it is likely to be for a long time to come, the disadvantages on this score would be greater than they may at first appear. But it must be admitted that they are far less than those that present themselves under the other aspects of the subject.

Upon the whole, there can be no room to doubt that the Convention acted wisely in following the models of those constitutions that have established good behavior as the tenure of their judicial offices, as regards duration. Far from being blamable on this account, their plan would have been inexcusably defective if it had lacked this important feature of good government. The experience of Great Britain offers an illustrious commentary on the excellence of the institution.
